What

What Deadwood Removal Involves

Deadwood removal — called "cleaning" under the ANSI A300 pruning standard — is the selective removal of dead, dying, diseased, and broken branches from an otherwise healthy tree. It is the lowest-impact pruning class because the crew is only taking wood the tree has already abandoned; no live tissue is cut. The primary driver is hazard mitigation: dead branches over walkways, driveways, parked vehicles, decks, or play areas.

The distinction that matters: this is maintenance pruning, not removal. The tree stays. Roubic works the interior and canopy to A300 standards, chips the brush, and rakes the ground clean before leaving. The technique applies to trees of every size and species across NE Ohio — from a heritage oak to an EAB-affected mixed-species stand where isolated ash branches have died back.

Why

Four Reasons Homeowners Call Roubic for Deadwood

The scenarios Aaron walks most often across NE Ohio residential and estate properties.

Dead Branches Over a Target

Dead limbs hanging over a walkway, driveway, pool deck, or play area. The most common reason to schedule — and the most time-sensitive.

EAB-Isolated Deadwood

Emerald ash borer kills isolated ash branches inside a mixed-species canopy. The tree lives; the dead ash limbs come out.

Routine Mature-Canopy Upkeep

Mature trees self-shade and abandon interior branches. A cleaning pass every 2–3 years keeps deadwood load below hazard thresholds.

Paired With Crown Work

Deadwood removal folds neatly into a crown thinning or crown reduction visit on an estate or heritage-tree property.

Common Deadwood Questions

Deadwood Removal FAQ

Five things NE Ohio homeowners want to know before booking.

How often should deadwood be removed from mature trees?
Routine maintenance every 2–3 years on mature canopy. More frequent visits may be appropriate after major storms, or when EAB is killing isolated ash branches in a mixed-species canopy. Deadwood is also commonly added to any dormant pruning rotation as a supplemental task.
Can deadwood be removed any time of year?
Yes — deadwood removal can be performed in any season because we're only taking wood the tree has already abandoned. The exception is oak: any branch work April 1 through July 31 is off-limits to avoid exposing the tree to oak wilt vectors.
How much does deadwood removal cost?
Standalone deadwood removal typically runs $200–$800 per tree depending on size and access. When combined with crown thinning or crown reduction, deadwood removal is often included at no additional charge. Multi-tree contracts qualify for package savings.
Is deadwood removal ever an emergency?
Generally no — most deadwood removal is scheduled routine work. The exception is a large dead branch over a target showing visible signs of imminent failure — cracking at the base, or a fresh hanger over a walkway. Call {{global.phone}} for those cases.
Does removing deadwood harm the tree?
No. Cleaning is the lowest-impact pruning class under ANSI A300 because no living tissue is cut — only dead, dying, diseased, or broken branches come out. Done correctly, it reduces hazard and helps the tree seal over old branch collars without stressing the canopy.
